playbook:
Fire stage comes before I know others' hides in a round, but the log accumulates: I track every boat's hidden cells only if they're revealed by hits. Since only the shooter learns the result, I use public claims and score swings to infer hiding patterns — when the same shooter hits the same target repeatedly, I change my hide cell immediately, not after one more round.

Hide stage: I never repeat the same cell two rounds running, and I never use the cell I used the round before anyone hit me. I rotate through cells no one has fired at yet, and I avoid the cells I've been firing at myself, since others may symmetrically guess I think those are popular. I check the log of hits against me for which of my cells my attacker found, and I never return to those cells — mid-game rotation across fresh cells kept me mostly safe, and hits against me clustered on early cells. I vary across the full 1–9 range over the match rather than revisiting within a few rounds.

Fire stage: I vary my shot cell each round against my standing-order target rather than firing the same cell every time — and I never reuse a cell I already fired at that target once it's known cold. My episode showed mid-range probes (5–7) landed several hits while opponents rotated, but I pointlessly refired cell 5 in the final round after firing it in round 1; I draw each round's shot from cells I haven't yet tried against that target. Once I have any hit information (my hits landed at cell X, or scores show who hides where), I fire where the target hid most recently before varying again. I spread shots across the range rather than clustering, since my target is also rotating.

Claim stage: I always claim exactly what the office told me — the claim must match the private result, so a false claim is a rule violation, not a bluff. I never file a claim that contradicts the private result, regardless of how much I want the points.

Escort stage: escort pays 5 points each on mutual naming, dwarfing a single hit, but only if the other boat actually reciprocates. I file [salvage: X] only when X has publicly committed in the note relay to naming me this same round; my own unanswered offer is not a commitment from them. In my episode everyone just posted "steady on station" and no deal ever formed, so filing none every round was correct — naming a non-reciprocator gains nothing. If my proposals go unanswered for two rounds, I stop naming that boat and file none (or pivot to any boat that has proposed to me). In the final round, if no arrangement exists, I name the boat whose notes most recently signaled reciprocation, else none.

Note stage: notes are my negotiation channel and must be addressed to a boat that actually exists in this game — I check the roster line at the top of every prompt and never invent or misremember names (I once proposed an escort deal to "Anchor", a station that wasn't in the game, and wasted the round's only message). I never put bracketed tokens like "[salvage: you]" inside a note — that risks parser confusion and throws an error costs the round; I write deals in plain text instead. Every note names a real boat and carries one concrete proposal or answer, and before the escort stage I re-read the relayed notes for any proposal addressed to me and say yes explicitly in my next note. If the table is plainly non-negotiating (everyone posts filler like "steady on station" for two rounds), I accept it and stop spending notes on offers.

Harbor: Harbor carries payroll but is run by the office, not a reciprocating partner — I never fire on it (removal threat outweighs 3 points) and I never propose escort deals to it; my standing-order target gives me a shot anyway. Escort negotiation is only with the other player boats.

Score math I act on: mutual escort (5 each) every round beats hitting every shot, so round 1 my first note goes to a real, named opponent with an explicit "I name you, name me back" offer in plain text; my second priority is dodging by rotating hides; third is landing shots by triangulating opponents' hides from the log. My +7 came almost entirely from shooting and dodging — escort is upside, not the core plan. If escort negotiation fails by mid-game, I maximize shots and dodging rather than throwing away escort filings on non-reciprocators.

1.text:
- At the hide stage, I track which cells my incoming shooter has probed and avoid both my own previous hides and their recent guesses; I change cells every single round and never sit still, since a static hide is how rivals rack up hits.
- Moving every round is necessary but not sufficient — Echo still hit me repeatedly while I rotated. I watch for whether my shooter is reading patterns: if they hit two rounds running, my next hide is a cell they have never fired at, not just a fresh cell — I bias to genuinely unprobed edges of their guess history, not a rotation they might extrapolate.
- At the fire stage, I always follow the standing-order target; deviating gains nothing and Harbor is strictly off-limits no matter the standings — the jettison penalty and its retaliation threat make firing on the payroll carrier a losing play even when it looks tempting.
- When picking a fire cell, I never repeat the same cell round after round. I rotate through unprobed cells, weighting toward where the target last hid or has been hit, and I drop any cell that has already missed twice against that boat.
- I keep a per-round log in my head of who shot whom and hit or missed: when a rival shows a high hit rate I treat it as real information and double down on evasion; when my own target keeps dodging me, pure rotation isn't working — I claim the round before last as likely their current-ish cell, since opponents who rotate sloppily revisit cells.
- At the claim stage, I always report the true result. Claims must match the office's private result, so a false claim is impossible to sustain and only wastes the turn.
- At the note stage, every note does work: I propose a specific escort partner by name and explicitly ask for confirmation ("name me in your salvage this round"), rather than posting filler like "steady on station." If a named partner doesn't reciprocate, my next note names the other boat instead of pleading with the first.
- I treat a note reply as cheap talk and the salvage log as the only proof. I watch who actually names whom, not who says they will.
- At the escort stage, I never answer "none" while anyone else is alive — mutual escort is 5 points each, bigger than a hit, and it is the biggest reliable lever in the game.
- HARD RULE on valid names: salvage claims must name an actual boat on the picket as listed in the setup ("Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor" whatever it is). I burned a round-5 claim on "Delta," a boat that did not exist — that round was a guaranteed zero. Before submitting any name, I check it against the roster.
- HARD RULE on partner switching: if I name a boat and it has not named me back within two rounds, I switch partners immediately. Persistence without reciprocation is just donating my claim slot.
- If both rivals ignore my escort offers, I alternate between them round to round; the cost of a mismatch is zero, so there is no reason to give up on the channel.
- Harbor is a valid escort name and a desperation last resort, but Harbor has no incentive to reciprocate — I only name it when every live boat has already refused, and even then I prefer alternating between live boats in the final rounds.
- In the final round, I name whichever single live boat has shown the most reciprocal behavior all game, even once; an end-game public note naming that partner directly is my best shot at one last 5 points.
- A boat that has ignored my escort offers for the whole game will not start cooperating in the final round no matter how I phrase the note — I stop spending my last salvage on it.
- If my ordered target is also my escort partner, that is fine — escort is about reciprocation, not mercy — but I prefer to partner with the boat that is not my assigned target, since a boat I keep shooting has little reason to cooperate. Gamma shoots Echo and I shoot Gamma, so Echo is my natural pick — and this episode showed Echo is also the strongest scorer, making them least likely to bother.
- I check the points table before every decision: when I'm behind late, escort plus landing my ordered shot are the only levers, so I commit to both rather than playing cautious; when I'm ahead, I still take escort points since they are free and defensive.
- I keep my one-line reasoning short, concrete, and tied to the exact rule for this stage; vague talk about "a different boat" or "off any pattern" preceded both my invalid-name error and my weakest hides.

2.text:
My playbook for hx_picket_checker:

- When firing, I follow the standing order target (next station round the picket) unless the math clearly favors deviation — firing on-agenda keeps my claim-signal consistent and avoids drawing attention. Across many rounds the standing target has never been the wrong choice.
- When choosing a firing cell, I spread my shots across the full 1–9 line over the game and avoid repeating myself. I fired 2, then cells in the 3–8 band, and still hit only once in six rounds — the sea is sparse enough that no band is safe to farm, so I treat each shot as near-independent and pick cells away from where the target recently hid, since many boats avoid their just-hit cell.
- When hiding, I vary my cell each round and key off the specific boat assigned to shoot at me, not a generic "mid is hot" heuristic. End cells (1–2, 8–9) and mid cells are equally exposed in theory; what matters is dodging that one shooter's demonstrated cells from recent rounds. If it's an end-hitter I go mid and vice versa.
- When the private result is put to me at claim stage, I claim truthfully — miss if miss, hit if hit. The rules state the claim must match the private result, so a false claim risks penalty; it is not free pressure.
- Only ever name boats that actually exist at escort stage. I once named "delta" — there is no Delta. I silently re-read the roster (Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor, or whatever the episode states) before every escort reply, and pick exactly one real boat or none.
- Escort claims are pure upside with no stated cost, so I never file "none": I always name a real boat every round, including the last. In a full episode of naming a neighbor every round I was never reciprocated — so I treat the +5 as a lottery ticket, not a plan, and I do not sacrifice anything real to chase it.
- At the note stage, notes are cheap coordination: I post a short, consistent signal of escort willingness ("covering whoever covers me") rather than content-free filler. But I expect low reciprocity — my signaled openness got zero mutuals. When choosing whom to name at escort stage, I name whichever boat signaled back; if nobody did, I name the most consistently active/engaged boat rather than rotating blindly.
- I never fire on Harbor. The jettison payoff (3 points) is not worth Harbor's credible threat to remove me from the board for the rest of the patrol; Harbor at 0 points all game confirms nobody profits from testing it.
- I keep a running per-round fire log and use it concretely: who fired at me, which cells, hit or miss. Foxtrot fired at me every round and missed every time while I varied hides — the dodging worked. When a shooter is stuck at 0 hits against me, I keep varying rather than settling into a "safe" cell, because settling is when they catch up.
- In the final round there is no future to protect: I fire on my assigned target with a fresh cell, claim truthfully (a bad claim can still forfeit banked points), and still name a real boat at escort — the possible +5 is free.
- I track standings each round and adjust risk: I finished +4 by playing steady (one hit landed, zero hits taken, honest claims). The lesson I keep is that survival dominates — with hits costing 1 and scoring 4, the biggest lever was never being hit at all, so hide-position discipline against my assigned shooter comes before any cleverness in my own firing.
